summary: Bad-luck protection: each failed roll raises the effective chance until a success is guaranteed.
problem: Independent random rolls produce streaks, and streaks feel like cheating even when the maths is honest. At a 5% drop rate, roughly one player in three still has nothing after 20 attempts and one in a hundred has nothing after 90 — and those are the players who post about it. A pity timer keeps the headline odds but puts a hard ceiling on the worst case: every failure nudges the chance up, and after a set number of failures the next roll simply succeeds. It is a plain C# class rather than a MonoBehaviour so a loot system can hold a dozen independent counters (one per table, one per rarity tier) as ordinary fields without spawning a GameObject for each.

params.why: The success chance on a roll with no accumulated failures — the floor the escalation builds from.
params.tuning: Set it BELOW your advertised drop rate. Because every subsequent roll is strictly more likely than this, the observed rate always comes out higher than baseChance. For a '5% drop' that actually measures near 5%, start noticeably lower and simulate.

params.why: The hard ceiling: once this many consecutive failures have accumulated, the next roll succeeds outright. It also sets how fast the chance ramps, since the escalation is FailCount / guaranteedAfter.
params.tuning: Pick it from the player experience you want to cap, not from the maths — 'nobody should ever go more than 20 pulls dry'. Small values (under about 5) make the ramp so steep that baseChance barely matters; 1 or 0 make every roll succeed.

workedExample.setup: The default configuration — a 5% base chance with a 20-attempt guarantee — traced as failures accumulate.
steps: Below the guarantee, chance = baseChance + (1 - baseChance) * FailCount / guaranteedAfter.
FailCount 19: the branch `FailCount >= guaranteedAfter — 1` fires first, so chance is forced to 1.0 — the formula's own 0.9525 is never used.
On a success FailCount resets to 0; on a failure it increments.
workedExample.result: The 20th roll after 19 straight failures always succeeds, so no player can ever go more than 20 attempts without a hit. Note the halfway point is already better than a coin flip — the average number of rolls per success is far below 20, and the realised drop rate is well above the 5% baseChance.

useCases: Gacha and loot-box pulls where a published pity count is part of the design contract with players.
Rare enemy drops, so a farming session cannot run dry indefinitely.
Critical-hit or dodge chances in a combat system, to smooth out runs that feel unfair.
Procedural events (a wandering merchant, a treasure room) that should show up eventually rather than statistically.
Any tuned probability where the worst case, not the average, is what generates complaints.

usage.codeNote: The two-argument constructor is the only way to configure it in code — baseChance and guaranteedAfter are private [SerializeField] with no setters. Declared as a serialized field, it also shows up in the Inspector because the class is [System.Serializable].

apiNotes.FailCount: Consecutive failures since the last success. Read-only from outside (private setter) — useful for a '12 / 20 to guaranteed' UI readout.
apiNotes.Roll(): Computes the escalated chance, rolls it via ProbabilityUtils.Chance, then either resets FailCount to 0 (success) or increments it (failure). One call per attempt — calling it twice rolls twice.
apiNotes.Reset(): Zeroes FailCount. The only mutator besides Roll(); use it when a new pity cycle should start (a new banner, a new season, a difficulty change).

gotchas.title: The realised drop rate is always higher than baseChance
gotchas.body: Every roll after the first uses a chance strictly greater than baseChance, and the guarantee caps the tail. So if a design document says '5% drop rate', typing 0.05 into baseChance produces something meaningfully more generous. Decide whether baseChance or the observed rate is the number you are balancing against, and simulate a few thousand rolls to check.

gotchas.title: Pity progress persists, via a serialized field
gotchas.body: FailCount was an auto-property with a private setter and therefore invisible to Unity's serializer — config survived a save and the player's accumulated bad luck did not, which is exactly backwards for the gacha case. It is now a [SerializeField] behind a read-only property, with LoadFailCount to restore it from a save (clamped, so a stored value cannot make the next roll a certainty).

gotchas.title: guaranteedAfter is clamped to at least 1
gotchas.body: At 0 the guarantee test read `0 >= -1`, true on a brand-new timer, so every roll succeeded and baseChance was ignored — verified at 1000 successes in 1000 rolls. It now clamps to 1, which means "guaranteed within one attempt" and so still always succeeds — that is the coherent reading of the value, not a bug. Anything below 2 makes baseChance irrelevant.

gotchas.title: Roll() draws from the global UnityEngine.Random stream
gotchas.body: It calls ProbabilityUtils.Chance, which uses UnityEngine.Random.value. Results are therefore not reproducible from a seed you control, and are affected by anything else in the frame that consumes the global stream. A PityTimer cannot be driven by a SeededRandom without reimplementing Roll().

gotchas.title: One counter per independent thing
gotchas.body: Sharing a single PityTimer across several loot tables couples them: a hit on one resets the pity for all. Give each table, tier or banner its own instance — which is exactly why it is a lightweight serializable class rather than a component.
